etymology: A pun from late-1980s hip-hop and street speech: Audi sounds like "outta" (as in "I’m outta here"), and the Audi 5000 was the German luxury sedan sold in America through the 1980s. "I’m Audi 5000" or simply "Audi 5000!" meant "I’m leaving, goodbye"; it merged in the early 1990s with outtie to give I’m outtie 5000. The car brand itself takes its name from the Latin audi, "listen!" — a Latin rendering of its founder August Horch’s surname (German horch, hark).
biblical_def: "I’m Audi 5000" is a Gen X goodbye with a grin: "Class is over — I’m Audi." The joke is a sound-alike: Audi for "outta," and the sleek 1980s sedan for the speed of the exit. It is a harmless phrase, and a father has no reason to scold it. But every goodbye is a small rehearsal for the larger ones, and Scripture is wise about departures. "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven" (Ecc 3:1) — a time to arrive and a time to go. The believer’s comings and goings are watched over: "The LORD shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in from this time forth, and even for evermore" (Psa 121:8). Our Lord used His own departure to comfort His disciples: "I go to prepare a place for you" (Joh 14:2). And Paul faced the last goodbye with something close to eagerness: "having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better" (Php 1:23); "the time of my departure is at hand" (2Ti 4:6). That is the Christian’s final I’m outta here — not an escape but a homecoming. A father can use the slang at the door and the theology at the bedside: leave a room well, say goodbye kindly, and live so that when your last departure comes you can say with Paul that you have finished your course and kept the faith.
webster_summary: Late-1980s hip-hop pun (Audi = "outta," after the 1980s Audi 5000 sedan) for "I’m leaving"; Scripture watches over every going out (Psa 121:8) and calls the believer’s last departure far better (Php 1:23).
webster_full: AUDI 5000, interj. (Gen X slang, late 1980s–1990s, hip-hop and street speech) I’m leaving; goodbye; I’m out of here. "Bell just rang — I’m Audi 5000."
Shortened to Audi; blended with outtie as I’m outtie 5000. A sound-alike pun on "outta" and the 1980s Audi 5000 sedan.
Companions: I’m out, let’s jet, peace out, later.
No entry in Webster 1828; the phrase is a late-20th-century American pun on a car model.
Decode for parents: "Audi 5000" just means goodbye; use it to teach that the LORD keeps our going out and coming in (Psa 121:8).
scriptures: Ecc 3:1
To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven:
The LORD shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in from this time forth, and even for evermore.
Joh 14:2
In my Father's house are many mansions: if it were not so, I would have told you. I go to prepare a place for you.
Php 1:23
For I am in a strait betwixt two, having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better:
For I am now ready to be offered, and the time of my departure is at hand.
corruption_summary: Audi 5000 is a harmless goodbye; its only shadow is a culture of quick exits that never learns to leave well — Scripture keeps every going out under God’s eye and makes the last departure a homecoming.
corruption_paragraphs: The quick exit. The phrase celebrates speed: gone before anyone can ask a question. Most of the time that is just fun. But a generation that perfected the quick exit also perfected the unanswered call, the dropped friendship, and the marriage walked out of without a word. Scripture teaches that there is a time to depart (Ecc 3:1), and it implies there is a way: with honesty, with thanks, and with the bridges left standing. The LORD who preserves our going out (Psa 121:8) cares how we go.

The last goodbye. Every I’m outta here is a small picture of the final one. For the unbeliever it is the darkest word in the language; for the Christian it is a door. Christ went ahead to prepare a place (Joh 14:2), and Paul could call his departure "far better" (Php 1:23). A child who learns that early will say goodbye at the door more lightly, and at the graveside with hope.

etymology: From out (as in "I’m out of here") with the playful -ie ending; African-American and hip-hop speech of the early 1990s, often extended to I’m outtie 5000 by blending with the earlier pun Audi 5000. By the mid-1990s it was ordinary teen and college slang for "I’m leaving," alongside peace out and I’m out.
biblical_def: "I’m outtie" is a cheerful announcement that you are leaving: "It’s late — I’m outtie." It is a happy little word, and there is nothing wrong with it. But it raises a question Scripture takes seriously: when should a person leave? The Bible’s heroes are often people who knew exactly when to say I’m out. When Potiphar’s wife grabbed Joseph, "he left his garment in her hand, and fled, and got him out" (Gen 39:12) — the most honorable exit in the Old Testament. The angels hurried Lot from Sodom: "Escape for thy life; look not behind thee" (Gen 19:17). Proverbs tells a young man what to do with the path of the wicked: "Avoid it, pass not by it, turn from it, and pass away" (Pro 4:15). Paul tells Timothy, "Flee also youthful lusts: but follow righteousness, faith, charity, peace" (2Ti 2:22), and promises that in every temptation God "will with the temptation also make a way to escape" (1Co 10:13). Sometimes the bravest thing a teenager can say is "I’m outtie" — to the party that turned, the website that opened, the conversation that went dark. That is not cowardice; it is Joseph’s courage. A father can give his son and daughter a standing permission and a code word: if you ever need to leave, call me and say you’re outtie, and I will come, no questions asked until morning.
webster_summary: Early-1990s hip-hop and teen slang (from "out" + -ie; also outtie 5000) for "I’m leaving"; Scripture honors the holy exit — Joseph fled and got him out (Gen 39:12), and God makes a way to escape (1Co 10:13).
webster_full: I’M OUTTIE, interj. (Gen X slang, early 1990s, African-American and hip-hop speech) I’m leaving; goodbye. "Movie’s over — I’m outtie."
Extended: I’m outtie 5000 (blending Audi 5000); shortened: outtie, I’m out.
Companions: peace out, let’s jet, later. Not to be confused with outie, a protruding navel.
No entry in Webster 1828; the form is late-20th-century American slang.
Decode for parents: give your children a code word for leaving a bad situation — and praise the exit like Joseph’s (Gen 39:12).
scriptures: And she caught him by his garment, saying, Lie with me: and he left his garment in her hand, and fled, and got him out.

And it came to pass, when they had brought them forth abroad, that he said, Escape for thy life; look not behind thee, neither stay thou in all the plain; escape to the mountain, lest thou be consumed.
Pro 4:15
Avoid it, pass not by it, turn from it, and pass away.
Flee also youthful lusts: but follow righteousness, faith, charity, peace, with them that call on the Lord out of a pure heart.

There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it.
corruption_summary: I’m outtie is an innocent goodbye; the Christian question is when to say it — Scripture praises the holy exit from temptation and promises a way to escape.
corruption_paragraphs: Staying too long. Youth culture is good at leaving boring places and bad at leaving dangerous ones. The pressure of the crowd keeps a young person in the room long after conscience has said go. Lot lingered in Sodom until the angels took him by the hand; his wife looked back. Proverbs’ four quick verbs — avoid it, pass not by it, turn from it, pass away (Pro 4:15) — are a drill for the moment when staying feels easier than leaving.

Joseph’s courage. Flight is not always weakness. Joseph left his cloak and his reputation in the hands of a liar rather than sin against God (Gen 39:12), and God honored him. Paul tells young Timothy to flee youthful lusts and then to follow righteousness (2Ti 2:22): the exit is the first half of obedience. God’s faithful promise (1Co 10:13) means there is always a door; I’m outtie may be the words that walk through it.

etymology: From jet, a forceful stream (Old French jeter, to throw; Latin iactare), which gave the 1940s jet engine and jet airliner; to jet, to travel fast, follows in mid-century American speech. In late-1980s and 1990s hip-hop and teen slang it became a casual word for leaving quickly: "I gotta jet," "Let’s jet." It is unrelated to jet, the black mineral (as in "jet-black"), which comes from Gagai in Asia Minor.
biblical_def: "I gotta jet" means I have to leave, and fast. The picture is a jet airliner — here one second, gone the next. Gen X loved speed in its words as in its music, and jet fit perfectly. The Christian observation is that Scripture has two things to say about haste, and they are both worth teaching a child. The first is a warning: "he that hasteth with his feet sinneth" (Pro 19:2). Hurry can be a vice — the rush that skips thinking, the dash out the door that leaves a chore undone and a mother unthanked. The second is a command: some things deserve all the speed we have. "I made haste, and delayed not to keep thy commandments" (Psa 119:60). When Jesus looked up into the sycamore and said, "Zacchaeus, make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house" (Luk 19:5), the little man jetted: "he made haste, and came down, and received him joyfully" (Luk 19:6). Behind both lies a sober fact: our lives themselves are jetting by. "It is soon cut off, and we fly away" (Psa 90:10); "what is your life? It is even a vapour" (Jas 4:14). A father can laugh when his son says he has to jet, and then teach him the difference: don’t rush past people, don’t hurry into sin — but when Christ calls, come down quickly, and receive Him joyfully.
webster_summary: Gen X slang (late 1980s–1990s, from the jet airliner) for leaving quickly; Scripture warns against sinful haste (Pro 19:2) and commends the haste of Zacchaeus coming down to Christ (Luk 19:6).
webster_full: JET, v. (Gen X slang, late 1980s–1990s) To leave, especially quickly. "I gotta jet — my mom’s waiting." "Let’s jet."
From the jet engine and jet airliner (1940s onward); earlier jet, a forceful spurt, from Old French jeter, to throw.
Companions: I’m outtie, Audi 5000, bounce, peace out. Unrelated to jet, the black mineral.

Webster 1828: JET, v.i. [See the Noun.] To shoot forward; to shoot out; to project; to jut; to intrude. 1. To strut; to throw or toss the body in haughtiness. 2. To jerk; to jolt; to be shaken. [This orthography is Rarely used. See Jut.]
Decode for parents: "I gotta jet" is just goodbye; teach the difference between hurrying past people and hastening to obey (Psa 119:60).
scriptures: Pro 19:2
Also, that the soul be without knowledge, it is not good; and he that hasteth with his feet sinneth.
I made haste, and delayed not to keep thy commandments.
Luk 19:5
And when Jesus came to the place, he looked up, and saw him, and said unto him, Zacchaeus, make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house.
Luk 19:6
And he made haste, and came down, and received him joyfully.
Jas 4:14
Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away.
corruption_summary: Jet prizes the fast getaway; Scripture distinguishes the sinful haste that rushes past wisdom from the holy haste that runs to obey, and reminds us our whole life is flying away.
corruption_paragraphs: The hurried life. Gen X grew up with jet travel, fast food, and the remote control; its children have the instant message. Speed became a virtue in itself. But Proverbs pairs haste with ignorance: the soul without knowledge and the feet that hurry (Pro 19:2) belong together. A family always jetting from one thing to the next has no time to think, to pray, or to listen. The slower virtues — patience, attention, thanksgiving — are the first casualties of the rush.

Make haste, and come down. Yet Scripture has its own urgency. The Psalmist hurried to obey (Psa 119:60), and Zacchaeus scrambled down from the tree the moment Jesus called his name (Luk 19:5-6). Life is a vapour (Jas 4:14), and the call of Christ is not one to answer later. The Christian is meant to be slow to sin and quick to repent — to jet away from evil and jet toward the Savior.

etymology: From Cheddar, the village in Somerset, England, whose cheese has carried the name since the 1600s. As slang for money, cheddar is a 1990s hip-hop extension of cheese (money), which some connect with the "government cheese" distributed through federal surplus programs from 1981; the yellow-orange of the cheese and the stacking of bricks of it suit the image. Cheddar, cheese, bread, dough, and scrilla all ran together in late-1990s rap.
biblical_def: Cheddar is money, especially the kind you stack and show: "He’s got cheddar." "I’m out here getting this cheddar." The slang is playful — it turns cash into something you can eat — but the songs that made it popular were usually about wanting more of it. The Christian observation is that God speaks about money more plainly than almost any other subject. Money is not evil; "the love of money is the root of all evil" (1Ti 6:10). The heart cannot be split: "Ye cannot serve God and mammon" (Mat 6:24). The hunger is never fed: "He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver" (Ecc 5:10). The cure is not a vow of poverty but contentment rooted in a promise: "be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee" (Heb 13:5). Agur’s prayer is the wisest financial plan in the Bible: "give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with food convenient for me" (Pro 30:8). Cheddar is an apt picture after all: it feeds you, it ages, and eventually it goes bad. A father should teach his son to work hard and earn well — and to hold his cheddar with an open hand, give the first of it to God, share it with the poor, and never let it become the thing he chases. The man who has Christ has the treasure; the money is just groceries for the road.
webster_summary: 1990s hip-hop slang for money (from cheese, perhaps "government cheese"); Scripture does not condemn money but the love of it (1Ti 6:10), and teaches contentment under God’s promise (Heb 13:5).
webster_full: CHEDDAR, n. (Gen X slang, 1990s, hip-hop) Money, cash, especially in quantity. "He’s stacking cheddar."
Extended from cheese (money); kin to bread, dough, scrilla, paper, Benjamins.
The cheese itself is named for Cheddar, Somerset, England; the slang may echo the 1980s "government cheese" of federal surplus programs.
No entry in Webster 1828; cheddar as money is late-20th-century American slang.
Decode for parents: "cheddar" is money talk; teach your children to earn it, give it, and never love it (1Ti 6:10).
scriptures: For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows.
Mat 6:24
No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon.
Ecc 5:10
He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he that loveth abundance with increase: this is also vanity.
Heb 13:5
Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.
Pro 30:8
Remove far from me vanity and lies: give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with food convenient for me:
corruption_summary: Cheddar makes money playful and the chase for it glamorous; Scripture blesses honest gain but names the love of money a root of all evil and offers contentment in God instead.
corruption_paragraphs: The stack as a goal. Late-1990s rap made getting money the plot of the song: the stack, the chain, the car, the crowd. Children absorb the plot more than the slang. Scripture’s diagnosis is exact: those who covet after money "have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows" (1Ti 6:10). The chase does not end, because silver never satisfies the man who loves it (Ecc 5:10).

Two masters. Our Lord did not say it is hard to serve God and money; He said it cannot be done (Mat 6:24). The Christian answer is not contempt for money but a change of master. Contentment (Heb 13:5) is possible because God has promised never to leave; Agur’s prayer (Pro 30:8) asks for enough, not for more. A household that gives first, saves wisely, and spends gratefully teaches its children who sits on the throne.

etymology: From the portrait of Benjamin Franklin on the U.S. hundred-dollar bill (on the $100 since 1914). Benjamins for hundred-dollar bills, and for money in general, circulated in 1990s hip-hop and was made a national catchphrase by Puff Daddy & the Family’s "It’s All About the Benjamins" (1997, on No Way Out). The forename goes back to the patriarch Benjamin, youngest son of Jacob; the Hebrew name means "son of the right hand."
biblical_def: Benjamins are hundred-dollar bills, named for Franklin’s face, and by extension money in quantity: "It’s all about the Benjamins." Puff Daddy’s 1997 hit turned the phrase into a creed for a decade of excess. The Christian observation begins with a small irony. The name on those bills first belonged to a baby born in sorrow on the road to Bethlehem: his dying mother named him Benoni, "but his father called him Benjamin" (Gen 35:18) — son of the right hand. The Bible’s Benjamin was a gift of love, not a stack of cash. Our Lord answered the creed of the song before it was written: "Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man’s life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth" (Luk 12:15). "What shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?" (Mar 8:36). The treasure worth stacking is stored elsewhere: "lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt" (Mat 6:20). And the most expensive transaction in history was not paid in Benjamins at all: "ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold … But with the precious blood of Christ" (1Pe 1:18-19). A father can tell his son: it is not all about the Benjamins. It is all about the Son at the right hand of God, who bought you with something no bank can print.
webster_summary: Hip-hop slang (1990s; Puff Daddy’s "It’s All About the Benjamins," 1997) for hundred-dollar bills, after Franklin’s portrait; Scripture answers that a man’s life consisteth not in his possessions (Luk 12:15) and that we were redeemed not with silver and gold (1Pe 1:18).
webster_full: BENJAMINS, n. pl. (Gen X slang, 1990s, hip-hop) Hundred-dollar bills; money in quantity. "It’s all about the Benjamins."
From Benjamin Franklin’s portrait on the $100 bill; also Benji, Franklins, C-notes.
Fixed in the culture by Puff Daddy & the Family, "It’s All About the Benjamins" (1997). Companion: cheddar.
No entry in Webster 1828; the slang plural is late-20th-century American.
Decode for parents: when the song says it’s all about the Benjamins, teach that it is all about the Son at God’s right hand.

Mar 8:36

Mat 6:20

But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot:
corruption_summary: "It’s all about the Benjamins" is a creed of covetousness; Scripture answers that a man’s life is not in his possessions and that the soul is bought only with the precious blood of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: A creed in a chorus. "It’s all about the Benjamins" was sung as a boast and heard as a philosophy. A generation of young men took it literally, measuring worth by the roll in the pocket. Our Lord’s warning was given to a man who wanted Jesus to settle an inheritance dispute: beware of covetousness, for life does not consist in abundance (Luk 12:15). The rich fool of the parable that follows died the night his barns were finished.

The price of a soul. Peter’s contrast is the deepest answer to the song. Silver and gold are "corruptible things" (1Pe 1:18); the price of redemption was "the precious blood of Christ" (1Pe 1:19). No stack of Benjamins can buy a soul, and no stack can keep one (Mar 8:36). The Christian can earn and use money freely because he knows exactly what it is worth — and what it is not.

etymology: Origin uncertain: often traced to French beau (sweetheart, beau) through Louisiana and Caribbean speech, or to baby talk. As a term of endearment — "my boo," a boyfriend, girlfriend, or spouse — it was current in African-American speech and in R&B and hip-hop by the early 1990s, and later spread to general American use (boo’d up, bae). It is unrelated to the boo! that startles or jeers.
biblical_def: Your boo is your sweetheart: "That’s my boo." It can mean a steady boyfriend or girlfriend, a fiancée, or a husband or wife of thirty years. As a pet name it is sweet and harmless, and many a godly couple has used it. The Christian observation is that Scripture has the richest vocabulary of love-names in all literature, and it attaches them to covenant. "My beloved is mine, and I am his" (Son 2:16) — belonging that runs both ways. "Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it" (Son 8:7). God built romance to live inside marriage, where it can last: "rejoice with the wife of thy youth" (Pro 5:18). Paul raises the bar higher than any love song: "Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it" (Eph 5:25). And he describes what such love looks like on an ordinary Tuesday: "Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not" (1Co 13:4). The question about boo is not the word but the bond. The culture uses it for a relationship with no promises, easily traded for the next one. Scripture says the one you call by a love-name should be the one you have covenanted with before God, or are honorably preparing to. A father can say to his daughter: one day a young man may call you his boo; make sure he is willing to call you his wife and to lay down his life for you, as Christ did for His bride.
webster_summary: Gen X / R&B slang (early 1990s; origin uncertain, perhaps French beau) for sweetheart, boyfriend, girlfriend, or spouse; Scripture’s love-names belong to covenant: my beloved is mine, and I am his (Son 2:16).
webster_full: BOO, n. (Gen X slang, early 1990s, African-American speech, R&B and hip-hop) Sweetheart; boyfriend or girlfriend; spouse. "Me and my boo are going to the movies."
Phrases: my boo, boo’d up (in a relationship), boo thang; later Millennial bae.
Perhaps from French beau; unrelated to the startling or jeering boo!
No entry in Webster 1828; the endearment is late-20th-century American slang.
Decode for parents: "boo" is a love-name; teach that love-names belong to covenant, not to a revolving door.
scriptures: Son 2:16
My beloved is mine, and I am his: he feedeth among the lilies.
Son 8:7
Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it: if a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned.
Pro 5:18
Let thy fountain be blessed: and rejoice with the wife of thy youth.
Eph 5:25
Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it;
Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up,
corruption_summary: Boo is a sweet love-name; the corruption is a culture that hands it out without covenant, while Scripture gives love-names their home in faithful, lifelong marriage.
corruption_paragraphs: Love-names without promises. Much of the music that popularized boo sang of romance that came and went with the seasons — this year’s boo, next year’s ex. The word was tender; the arrangement was not. Scripture’s love poetry is just as tender and far more serious: the Song of Solomon’s "my beloved is mine, and I am his" (Son 2:16) is the language of mutual possession, and its love is a seal that many waters cannot quench (Son 8:7).

A boo for life. The answer is not to forbid pet names but to fill them. Proverbs tells a husband to rejoice with the wife of his youth (Pro 5:18) — still delighting in her when both are gray. Paul makes the cross the measure of a husband’s love (Eph 5:25). Children who watch their parents call each other by sweet names, and keep their vows, learn what the word is for.
roots_summary: Perhaps French beau (sweetheart) → Louisiana / Caribbean speech → early-1990s R&B and hip-hop my boo → Millennial bae; Scripture: my beloved is mine, and I am his (Son 2:16).
roots_lines: Origin uncertain; perhaps French beau — handsome; a sweetheart
African-American and Southern speech: boo as a term of endearment
Early 1990s R&B and hip-hop: my boo, a sweetheart
2000s–2010s spread: boo’d up, bae
Biblical love-names: my beloved (Son 2:16); the wife of thy youth (Pro 5:18)
usage: "Happy anniversary to my boo of twenty years."
My beloved is mine, and I am his (Son 2:16).
Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church (Eph 5:25).

etymology: From short + -y; long an American nickname for a short man or a small child. In East Coast hip-hop and street speech of the late 1980s and early 1990s shorty (later also shawty, the Atlanta pronunciation popular in the 2000s) took two new senses: a younger kid or protégé ("my little shorty"), and, most commonly, a young woman or girlfriend. Usage ranges from affectionate to dismissive depending on the speaker.
biblical_def: In Gen X slang a shorty is either a younger kid who tags along — "Shorty, go home, your mom’s calling" — or, more often, a young woman: "Who’s that shorty?" The word can be affectionate, but in a great deal of 1990s rap it reduced a woman to her looks and her availability. The Christian observation begins with the oldest sense. Scripture’s most famous shorty is Zacchaeus, who "sought to see Jesus who he was; and could not for the press, because he was little of stature" (Luk 19:3) — and Jesus stopped under his tree and called him by name. God does not measure as men measure: "man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart" (1Sa 16:7). The young are not to be despised either: "Let no man despise thy youth" (1Ti 4:12); "despise not one of these little ones" (Mat 18:10). When the word is used of young women, Paul supplies the only right posture for a young man: treat "the younger as sisters, with all purity" (1Ti 5:2). That is the test. If a boy calls a girl shorty the way he would speak of his own sister — with warmth and protection — little harm is done. If he uses it the way the songs did, to size her up, he is looking on the outward appearance and forgetting she bears God’s image. A father can tell his son: there are no "shorties" in God’s eyes — only image-bearers, and every young woman is somebody’s daughter and maybe someone’s future wife.
webster_summary: Hip-hop slang (late 1980s–1990s, East Coast; later shawty) for a younger kid or, chiefly, a young woman; Scripture measures by the heart, not the stature (1Sa 16:7), and tells young men to treat young women as sisters, with all purity (1Ti 5:2).
webster_full: SHORTY, n. (Gen X slang, late 1980s–1990s, East Coast hip-hop and street speech) A young woman or girlfriend; also a younger kid, a protégé. "Who’s that shorty by the lockers?"
Variant shawty (Atlanta, 2000s). Older sense: a nickname for a short person.
Tone ranges from affectionate (little brother, little sister) to appraising and dismissive (a girl sized up by looks).
Webster 1828: SHORT, a. [Latin curtus.] 1. Not long; not having great length or extension; as a short distance; a short ferry; a short flight; a short piece of timber. …
Decode for parents: ask how your son means it; teach him to speak of young women as sisters, with all purity (1Ti 5:2).
scriptures: Luk 19:3
And he sought to see Jesus who he was; and could not for the press, because he was little of stature.

But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.
Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity.
The elder women as mothers; the younger as sisters, with all purity.
Take heed that ye despise not one of these little ones; for I say unto you, That in heaven their angels do always behold the face of my Father which is in heaven.
corruption_summary: Shorty can be warm, but in much hip-hop it sized up young women by looks and availability; Scripture measures by the heart and commands young men to treat young women as sisters, with all purity.
corruption_paragraphs: Sizing up. The trouble with shorty was never the height joke; it was the eye behind it. In many 1990s songs a shorty was a girl appraised and pursued, rarely a person known. That is the outward-appearance looking that God refused when Samuel admired Eliab (1Sa 16:7). A boy trained by the music to evaluate girls will find it hard to honor a wife. Paul’s rule — the younger as sisters, with all purity (1Ti 5:2) — turns the appraising eye into a protecting one.

The little ones. The older, kinder sense of the word survives in neighborhoods where a big kid looks out for his shorty. That instinct is good, and Jesus blesses it: despise not one of these little ones (Mat 18:10). Zacchaeus was the shorty of Jericho, mocked and pushed aside by the crowd, and he was the one Jesus went home with (Luk 19:3). God has a long record of choosing the overlooked.
roots_summary: English short → nickname shorty (a small man, a child) → late-1980s East Coast hip-hop shorty (young woman; younger kid) → Atlanta shawty; Scripture: the LORD looketh on the heart (1Sa 16:7).
roots_lines: Old English sceort → short; nickname shorty — a small man, a child
Late 1980s–early 1990s East Coast hip-hop: shorty — a young woman, a girlfriend
Also: a younger kid or protégé ("my little shorty")
2000s Atlanta: shawty spreads through Southern rap
Biblical measure: Zacchaeus, little of stature (Luk 19:3); the younger as sisters (1Ti 5:2)
usage: "Shorty, you can come with us, but stay close."
Man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart (1Sa 16:7).
The younger as sisters, with all purity (1Ti 5:2).

etymology: An African-American Vernacular pronunciation of player. In 1960s–70s street slang a player was a smooth hustler who lived by his wits, and, above all, a man who kept several women at once; the spelling playa spread through 1990s hip-hop, and "Don’t hate the player, hate the game" became a catchphrase by the end of the decade. Related: playa hater, pimpin’, mack.
biblical_def: A playa is a man who juggles women — dating several at once, saying what each wants to hear, and treating the whole business as a game he is winning. In 1990s rap and film the playa was a hero: smooth, well dressed, never caught, never committed. The Christian observation is that Scripture has a plain name for this, and it is not a compliment. "Whoso committeth adultery with a woman lacketh understanding: he that doeth it destroyeth his own soul" (Pro 6:32). "For this is the will of God, even your sanctification, that ye should abstain from fornication" (1Th 4:3). "Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge" (Heb 13:4). The playa thinks he is the winner of the game; Proverbs says he is the one being played — led like an ox to the slaughter. Job shows the opposite kind of man: "I made a covenant with mine eyes; why then should I think upon a maid?" (Job 31:1). Malachi calls a husband to guard his heart: "let none deal treacherously against the wife of his youth" (Mal 2:15). A Christian should drop the word as praise. The playa is not a model of manhood but its counterfeit; the real man keeps one covenant with one woman for life, and finds that a far better story. A father must say it plainly to his son: never admire a playa, never become one, and if you have played, run to Christ, who forgives the repentant and makes a faithful man out of an unfaithful one.
webster_summary: AAVE / hip-hop form of player (1990s) for a man who juggles women and treats romance as a game; Scripture calls it fornication or adultery and says he that doeth it destroyeth his own soul (Pro 6:32).
webster_full: PLAYA, n. (Gen X slang, 1990s, hip-hop and African-American vernacular) A man who romances several women at once, deceptively; a smooth ladies’ man; by extension, anyone slick and successful. "He thinks he’s a playa."
From player (1960s–70s street slang: hustler, womanizer); catchphrase "Don’t hate the player, hate the game."
Kin: playa hater (one who envies him), mack, pimpin’; verb to play a woman, to deceive her.

Webster 1828: PLAYER, n. One who plays in any game or sport. 1. An idler. 2. An actor of dramatic scenes; one whose occupation is to imitate characters on the stage. 3. A mimic. 4. One who performs on an instrument of music. 5. A gamester. 6. One that acts a part in a certain manner.
Decode for parents: "playa" celebrates serial seduction; teach your son that the faithful one-woman man is the real hero (Mal 2:15).
scriptures: Pro 6:32
But whoso committeth adultery with a woman lacketh understanding: he that doeth it destroyeth his own soul.
For this is the will of God, even your sanctification, that ye should abstain from fornication:
Heb 13:4
Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.
Job 31:1
I made a covenant with mine eyes; why then should I think upon a maid?
Mal 2:15

And did not he make one? Yet had he the residue of the spirit. And wherefore one? That he might seek a godly seed. Therefore take heed to your spirit, and let none deal treacherously against the wife of his youth.
corruption_summary: Playa turns serial seduction and deceit into a badge of manhood; Scripture names it fornication and treachery, and holds up the covenant-keeping man as the real thing.
corruption_paragraphs: A sin made glamorous. The playa of 1990s music and film was never shown at the end of the story: the abandoned children, the diseases, the loneliness at fifty. The word made a game of what God calls treachery (Mal 2:15) and taught boys that the number of girls was the measure of a man. Scripture tells the rest of the story: he lacketh understanding and destroyeth his own soul (Pro 6:32). "Flee fornication" (1Co 6:18) is not prudishness; it is a rescue.

The covenant man. Job’s covenant with his eyes (Job 31:1) is the opposite of the playa’s roving glance. Paul calls every believer to possess his own body "in sanctification and honour" (1Th 4:4), and Hebrews sets marriage as honourable in all (Heb 13:4). The gospel does not merely scold the playa; it forgives him and remakes him. Many a former playa has become a faithful husband and a watchful father by the grace of Christ.
roots_summary: English play → player → 1960s–70s street slang (hustler, womanizer) → 1990s hip-hop playa → "don’t hate the player"; Scripture: he that doeth it destroyeth his own soul (Pro 6:32).
roots_lines: Old English plegian — to play, to sport; player — one who plays
1960s–70s American street slang: player — a hustler; a man with many women
1990s hip-hop and AAVE spelling: playa; "playa hater"
Late 1990s catchphrase: "Don’t hate the player, hate the game"
Biblical verdict: abstain from fornication (1Th 4:3); deal not treacherously (Mal 2:15)
usage: "He’s got three girlfriends — thinks he’s a real playa."
Whoso committeth adultery … destroyeth his own soul (Pro 6:32).
I made a covenant with mine eyes (Job 31:1) — the anti-playa’s vow.

etymology: A hip-hop compound of the mid-1990s (also playa hater, verb playa-hatin’): one who resents and runs down another person’s success, style, or popularity. The Notorious B.I.G. recorded "Playa Hater" on Life After Death (1997), and the phrase was later lampooned in the "Player Haters’ Ball" sketches on Chappelle’s Show (2003). Shortened by the end of the 1990s to hater.
biblical_def: A player hater is someone who cannot stand to see another man do well: he mocks the new car, sneers at the girlfriend, whispers about the promotion. The slang assumed the success was admirable and the hater was small — and on the second point Scripture agrees completely. The sin underneath is envy, and the Bible is unsparing about it. "A sound heart is the life of the flesh: but envy the rottenness of the bones" (Pro 14:30). "Where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work" (Jas 3:16). Solomon saw that much of the world’s labor is driven by it: "for this a man is envied of his neighbour. This is also vanity and vexation of spirit" (Ecc 4:4). Paul warns believers not to be "provoking one another, envying one another" (Gal 5:26). Here the Bible adds something the slang missed. Asaph confessed, "I was envious at the foolish, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked" (Psa 73:3). Sometimes the "player" being hated is not admirable at all — and the believer’s temptation is to envy him anyway, to wish he had the playa’s freedom. "Let not thine heart envy sinners: but be thou in the fear of the LORD all the day long" (Pro 23:17). The cure for both kinds of envy is the same: go into the sanctuary, as Asaph did, and see the end of things; then rejoice with them that rejoice. A father can tell his son: don’t be a hater, and don’t envy the playa — love your brother’s good, and want God more than anything anyone else has.
webster_summary: Mid-1990s hip-hop compound (Notorious B.I.G., "Playa Hater," 1997) for one who resents another’s success; Scripture names the sin envy, the rottenness of the bones (Pro 14:30), and warns too against envying sinners (Psa 73:3).
webster_full: PLAYER HATER, n. (Gen X slang, mid-1990s, hip-hop) One who resents, mocks, or undermines another’s success, style, or popularity. "Don’t listen to him — he’s just a player hater."
Variants: playa hater; verb playa-hatin’; shortened to hater by the late 1990s.
The Notorious B.I.G., "Playa Hater" (Life After Death, 1997); Chappelle’s Show, "Player Haters’ Ball" (2003).
Webster 1828: HATER, n. One that hates. An enemy to God, and hater of all good.
Decode for parents: "player hater" names envy; teach your children to rejoice in others’ good and to envy no one, least of all sinners.
scriptures: A sound heart is the life of the flesh: but envy the rottenness of the bones.
Jas 3:16
For where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work.
Ecc 4:4
Again, I considered all travail, and every right work, that for this a man is envied of his neighbour. This is also vanity and vexation of spirit.
Gal 5:26
Let us not be desirous of vain glory, provoking one another, envying one another.
Psa 73:3
For I was envious at the foolish, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked.
corruption_summary: Player hater rightly mocks envy but assumes the player is worth envying; Scripture condemns envy at its root and warns the believer not to envy sinners at all.
corruption_paragraphs: Envy named, envy kept. The phrase was a clever defense: any criticism of the player could be waved off as hating. That made envy easy to name in others and hard to see in oneself, and it shielded the player from honest rebuke. Scripture does not let either side off. Envy rots the bones (Pro 14:30) and breeds confusion and every evil work (Jas 3:16); but a man’s success does not make his life right, and a friend’s warning is not hate.

Asaph’s cure. Psalm 73 is the Bible’s honest account of player-hating: a godly man nearly slipped because he envied the prosperity of the wicked (Psa 73:3). His cure was not to stop noticing but to go into the sanctuary of God and understand their end. A believer freed from envy can do what the hater cannot — rejoice with them that rejoice — because charity envieth not (1Co 13:4) and his treasure is safe in God.
roots_summary: Street player + English hater → mid-1990s hip-hop player hater → Biggie’s "Playa Hater" (1997) → hater → Chappelle’s "Player Haters’ Ball" (2003); Scripture: envy the rottenness of the bones (Pro 14:30).
roots_lines: Player (street slang: hustler, ladies’ man) + hater (one who hates)
Mid-1990s hip-hop: player hater, playa-hatin’
1997: The Notorious B.I.G., "Playa Hater," on Life After Death
Late 1990s: shortened to hater; 2003 Chappelle’s Show parody
Biblical diagnosis: envy (Pro 14:30; Gal 5:26); envying sinners (Psa 73:3; Pro 23:17)
usage: "Stop player-hatin’ just because he made varsity."
A sound heart is the life of the flesh: but envy the rottenness of the bones (Pro 14:30).
I was envious at the foolish, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked (Psa 73:3).

etymology: An old English word — hater, one who hates, in use since the Middle Ages and found in the Authorized Version’s "haters of God" (Rom 1:30). The slang sense, a person who resents or criticizes someone out of envy, was clipped from hip-hop’s player hater in the late 1990s and became general American slang in the 2000s, when "haters gonna hate" turned into a catchphrase for dismissing critics.
biblical_def: In slang a hater is anyone who criticizes you, especially out of jealousy: "Ignore the haters." "Haters gonna hate." Sometimes the label is accurate — envy is real, and some people do tear down what they cannot build. But the word has become a shield against every kind of correction, and that is where a Christian must examine it. Scripture says the man who refuses all criticism is the fool: "Whoso loveth instruction loveth knowledge: but he that hateth reproof is brutish" (Pro 12:1). "Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful" (Pro 27:6) — the person who tells you the hard truth may be your best friend, and the flatterer your enemy. "Rebuke a wise man, and he will love thee" (Pro 9:8). And when the opposition really is hatred, our Lord gives an answer no slogan can match: "Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you" (Mat 5:44). He also warns His people to expect it: "If the world hate you, ye know that it hated me before it hated you" (Joh 15:18). The old word has a sobering use in Paul’s list of human rebellion — "haters of God" (Rom 1:30) — which describes every one of us before grace. A father can teach his children two things: before you call someone a hater, ask whether he is telling you the truth; and when someone truly hates you, pray for him, for you too were once a hater of God, and Christ loved you anyway.
webster_summary: Late-1990s hip-hop clipping of player hater for an envious critic; Scripture warns that he that hateth reproof is brutish (Pro 12:1), commands love for real enemies (Mat 5:44), and keeps the old sense: haters of God (Rom 1:30).
webster_full: HATER, n. (Gen X slang, late 1990s–present, from hip-hop) One who resents, criticizes, or belittles another, especially out of envy. "Don’t worry about the haters."
Clipped from player hater; catchphrase "haters gonna hate" (2000s); verb to hate on.
Old sense, still standard: one who hates; the AV’s "haters of God" (Rom 1:30).
Webster 1828: HATER, n. One that hates. An enemy to God, and hater of all good.
Decode for parents: "hater" can name real envy, but it is often a shield against correction; teach your children to weigh criticism before dismissing it.
scriptures: Pro 12:1
Whoso loveth instruction loveth knowledge: but he that hateth reproof is brutish.
Pro 27:6
Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.
Mat 5:44
But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you;
If the world hate you, ye know that it hated me before it hated you.
Rom 1:30
Backbiters, haters of God, despiteful, proud, boasters, inventors of evil things, disobedient to parents,
corruption_summary: Hater can name real envy, but it has become a shield that dismisses every rebuke; Scripture prizes the faithful wounds of a friend and commands love for those who truly hate us.
corruption_paragraphs: The shield against correction. "Haters gonna hate" is a convenient creed: every critic becomes an envier, and the self never has to change. Proverbs calls that posture brutish (Pro 12:1) — the mind of a beast that cannot be taught. The friend who wounds you with the truth is faithful; the crowd that flatters you is not (Pro 27:6). A culture that labels every rebuke as hate raises children who cannot be corrected, and adults who cannot repent.

Loving the real haters. Jesus never told His disciples to ignore their haters; He told them to love, bless, and pray for them (Mat 5:44). He was hated first (Joh 15:18), and He died for those who hated Him. Paul’s word "haters of God" (Rom 1:30) describes all of us before grace. A Christian who remembers that cannot look down on anyone as a hater; he can only pray for him.
roots_summary: Middle English hater (one who hates; "haters of God," Rom 1:30) → hip-hop player hater (mid-1990s) → clipped hater (late 1990s) → "haters gonna hate" (2000s); Scripture: love your enemies (Mat 5:44).

1611 AV: "haters of God" (Rom 1:30)
Mid-1990s hip-hop: player hater — one who envies another’s success
Late 1990s–2000s: clipped hater; "haters gonna hate"
Biblical counsel: love reproof (Pro 12:1); love your enemies (Mat 5:44)
usage: "She only said that because she’s a hater."
Faithful are the wounds of a friend (Pro 27:6) — not every critic is a hater.
Love your enemies … do good to them that hate you (Mat 5:44).

etymology: An old English word: scrub, stunted brushwood, gave the 16th-century sense "a mean, insignificant fellow," and American sports slang of the late 1800s used scrub for a second-string player. Gen X revived it through TLC’s "No Scrubs" (1999, FanMail), which defined a scrub as a man with no money and no prospects who still wants a woman’s attention — "a guy that thinks he’s fly and is also known as a busta." Gamers later used scrub for an unskilled player.
biblical_def: A scrub, as TLC sang in 1999, is a man who has nothing going for him and acts as if he does: no job, no car, living off others, still calling out to girls from the passenger side of his friend’s ride. The song told young women to say no to him, and on the main point Scripture agrees. A grown man who will not work is not a romantic prospect; he is a sluggard. "If any would not work, neither should he eat" (2Th 3:10). "Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise" (Pro 6:6). A man who will not provide "hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel" (1Ti 5:8). And the diligent man has a future: "Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings" (Pro 22:29). So far, the song is wise. But the word needs examining, because it measures a man mostly by his money. Scripture warns against exactly that: James rebukes the church that seats "a man with a gold ring, in goodly apparel" in the best place and sends "a poor man in vile raiment" to the floor (Jas 2:2-3). A young man who is poor but hard-working, humble, and godly is not a scrub; he may be the best husband in the county. The real scrub is the lazy man, not the poor one. A father can tell his daughter: don’t marry a man who won’t work; and don’t despise a man just because he hasn’t made it yet — look for diligence and the fear of the LORD. He can tell his son: work, provide, and never be a scrub.
webster_summary: 1990s slang revived by TLC’s "No Scrubs" (1999) for a man with no job or prospects who still seeks attention; Scripture condemns the sluggard (2Th 3:10) but forbids measuring a man by his money (Jas 2:2-3).
webster_full: SCRUB, n. (Gen X slang, late 1990s; revived by TLC) A man with no money, job, or prospects who acts important and seeks women’s attention; a loser, a freeloader. "I don’t want no scrub."
TLC, "No Scrubs" (FanMail, 1999), which pairs it with busta; later gamer slang for an unskilled player.
Older senses: stunted brushwood; a mean, insignificant fellow (16th c.); a second-string player (US sports, late 1800s).
Webster 1828: SCRUB, n. 1. A mean fellow; one that labors hard and lives meanly. 2. Something small and mean. No little scrub joint shall come on my board. 3. A worn out brush.
Decode for parents: the song is right about lazy men, but teach your children to judge by diligence and godliness, not money.
scriptures: For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat.
Pro 6:6
Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise:
But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel.
Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings; he shall not stand before mean men.
Jas 2:2
For if there come unto your assembly a man with a gold ring, in goodly apparel, and there come in also a poor man in vile raiment;
corruption_summary: Scrub rightly mocks the lazy freeloader but measures a man chiefly by his money; Scripture condemns the sluggard and honors the diligent, yet forbids despising the poor.
corruption_paragraphs: Right about laziness. TLC’s song made a point the church should not be embarrassed to make: a man who will not work, will not provide, and still expects a woman’s devotion is not worth her yes. Paul says it more bluntly (2Th 3:10; 1Ti 5:8). A generation of young men raised without fathers often never learned to work, and the slang named the result. Proverbs’ ant (Pro 6:6) is still the best teacher.

Wrong about money. The danger in the word is that it slides from lazy to poor. A man is called a scrub because he has no car, no cash, no flash. James calls that partiality and sin (Jas 2:2-3). The godly young man with a modest job, a humble heart, and calloused hands is a prize, not a scrub. Diligence (Pro 22:29) and the fear of the LORD are the measure; the gold ring is not.
roots_summary: Middle English scrobbe (brushwood) → scrub, a mean fellow (16th c.) → US sports scrub (second-stringer) → TLC’s "No Scrubs" (1999) → gamer scrub; Scripture: go to the ant, thou sluggard (Pro 6:6).

16th c.: scrub — a mean, insignificant fellow
Late 1800s US sports: scrub — a substitute, a second-string player
1999: TLC, "No Scrubs" — a broke man who still wants attention
Biblical measure: if any would not work (2Th 3:10); diligent in his business (Pro 22:29)
usage: "He borrowed gas money again? What a scrub."
Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise (Pro 6:6).
A man with a gold ring … and … a poor man in vile raiment (Jas 2:2) — judge not by the ring.

etymology: An AAVE and hip-hop pronunciation of buster, which in older American slang was a contemptuous form of address ("Listen, buster"). In late-1980s and 1990s hip-hop a busta was a fake, a pretender, a coward who talks big and backs down, or a loser who tries too hard; TLC’s "No Scrubs" (1999) pairs it with scrub. The rapper Busta Rhymes reportedly took his stage name, at Chuck D’s suggestion, from the NFL receiver George "Buster" Rhymes.
biblical_def: A busta is a fake: the guy who talks tough and runs when it counts, who claims what he does not have, who says he’s down for his friends and is nowhere to be found when they need him. "Don’t be a busta." The word combines two failures — pretense and cowardice — and Scripture knows both well. On pretense: "Most men will proclaim every one his own goodness: but a faithful man who can find?" (Pro 20:6). "Let love be without dissimulation" (Rom 12:9) — without the mask. Our Lord’s sternest warning was for religious bustas: "Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father" (Mat 7:21). On cowardice: "Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong" (1Co 16:13). "Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee" (Jos 1:9). Notice where Joshua’s courage comes from — not from swagger but from the presence of God. That is the cure for the busta in every one of us. Peter talked big at the Last Supper and denied his Lord three times before dawn; he was the busta of the Gospels. Then Christ forgave him, filled him with the Spirit, and made him bold. A father can say to his son: don’t pretend to be more than you are, and don’t run when your friends or your faith need you; and if you have been a busta, so was Peter — go back to Jesus, and He will make you a man.
webster_summary: Hip-hop pronunciation of buster (late 1980s–1990s) for a fake, a pretender, a coward; Scripture asks, a faithful man who can find? (Pro 20:6) and commands quit you like men, be strong (1Co 16:13).
webster_full: BUSTA, n. (Gen X slang, late 1980s–1990s, hip-hop and AAVE) A fake, a pretender; a coward who talks big and backs down; a try-hard loser. "He ran when the fight started — straight busta."
From buster, an old contemptuous form of address; paired with scrub in TLC’s "No Scrubs" (1999).
Busta Rhymes’s stage name reportedly came from NFL receiver George "Buster" Rhymes. Companions: poser, wannabe, punk.
No entry in Webster 1828; the slang busta is late-20th-century American.
Decode for parents: "busta" means fake and fearful; teach courage that comes from God’s presence, not from swagger (Jos 1:9).

corruption_summary: Busta rightly scorns pretense and cowardice but answers them with more swagger; Scripture cures both with faithfulness and with courage drawn from the presence of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Swagger is not courage. Street culture feared being called a busta so much that young men proved themselves by fighting, by risk, and by never backing down — which often ended in a hospital or a cell. That is not courage but another kind of fear: fear of men’s opinion. Scripture’s courage is quieter and stronger. "Quit you like men" (1Co 16:13) is paired with "stand fast in the faith"; Joshua’s boldness rests on "the LORD thy God is with thee" (Jos 1:9).

Every man a busta. The honest Christian admits that he has been the fake and the coward. Most men proclaim their own goodness (Pro 20:6); Peter swore he would die for Jesus and then denied Him to a servant girl. The gospel’s answer is not shame but restoration: the risen Christ asked Peter three times, "Lovest thou me?" and gave him back his calling. Love without dissimulation (Rom 12:9) grows out of being forgiven.
